newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile forestry firms blast U.S. court ruling.
newsitem.headline: Chile forestry firms blast U.S. court ruling.

text.p: Chilean forestry companies Friday criticised a U.S. court ruling banning new import permits for logs and wood chips from Chile and two other countries, saying the order was a new form of protectionism.
"We consider that the measure is tremendously serious," Fernando Leniz, president of forestry lobby group Corporacion Chilena de la Madera (Corma), told a news conference.
"It is an extremely serious precedent for the obstruction of international trade."

A federal court in San Francisco upheld appeals by four U.S. environment groups from the East Coast against the granting of new permits to import pine logs and wood chips from Chile, New Zealand and Russia.

The court banned the Agriculture Department from issuing the new permits on the grounds that products from these countries have not been proved to be free of diseases that could infect North American trees.

The dispute is the second over trade in recent months between Chile and the United States. Chile is defending its salmon raisers against allegations of illegal subsidies in a dispute being analysed at the U.S. Trade Department.
Last year, Chile exported pine logs worth $12 million to the United States -- a small part of the forestry industry's total exports worth over $1.8 billion.
Chilean companies have written to the Agriculture Department to complain about the ruling, said Leniz.
The four Chilean firms who export logs and chips to the United States already have permits for this year, so the order will only have an impact in 1998, he said.
Company officials blasted the ruling as protectionist and said it could affect other products exported to the United States.

Chile's forestry industry has boomed in the last 20 years with thousands of acres of fast-growing pine and eucalyptus forests blanketing hills in the south. Some species, including North American pine, grow faster in Chile than in their native territory.
